newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Dubliner accused of Irish journalist's murder.
newsitem.headline: Dubliner accused of Irish journalist's murder.

text.p: A 32-year-old Dublin man was on Tuesday charged with the murder of Veronica Guerin, Ireland's top investigative reporter who was shot dead by a motorcyle pillion passenger in an apparent contract killing last June.
Paul Ward said nothing when the charge was read out to him at Kilmainham court in Dublin, police said.
He has been in custody for months on charges of conspiracy to murder Guerin but these were withdrawn when the new charge was laid against him.

Ward was one of half a dozen prisoners at Dublin's Mountjoy jail who held warders hostage for several days this year in a protest against conditions and the charges against them. They gave up their protest peacefully after several days.
Guerin was gunned down at the wheel of her car at a traffic lights outside Dublin by the passenger on a motorbike which drew up beside her and then sped away after the shooting.
Police believe her killers were hired to prevent publication of any further exposes about the Dublin criminal underworld.
She had for years specialised in stories about Ireland's murky gangland especially drug barons enriching themselves from a growing narcotic trade across the island of Ireland.
Her killing shocked the public and government and brought about new legislation empowering the authorites to seize money and property owned by suspected criminals.

Prime Minister John Bruton promised the nation that her murderers would not go free and police have questioned suspects in parts of Britain and Ireland in one of the biggest investigations ever mounted.
Guerin's murder was hailed as a tragedy by the International Press Institute, journalists and by her employers, the Independent Newspaper group.
She was the crime correspondent of the Sunday Independent.
Guerin was shot once before the June incident but said she would never give up her attempts to expose people living off the proceeds of crime.
Ireland has a growing drug problem. Heroin is widely available and the price has dropped as the drug has taken hold in low-income areas.
It is also a trans-shipment area for narcotics which are dropped into the ocean in waterproof bales and collected from unpoliced beaches and sent to Europe and elsewhere.
